sections.html:
Spartanburg, seat of Spartanburg County, sits in the Upstate about 98 miles northwest of Columbia and 80 miles west of Charlotte. The city had 38,732 residents in 2020, while the surrounding metro area counts 383,327. Your house is therefore part of a much larger market than the city's own population suggests.

The Hub City nickname comes from the railroad lines that once radiated from the town. Textile mills shaped the housing here, with around 40 mills established by the early 1900s, and some neighborhoods still show it.

• Downtown and Morgan Square: the original courthouse village and the city's main hub
  • Hampton Heights: the oldest intact downtown neighborhood, a historic district with Queen Anne, Neoclassical and bungalow homes
  • Northside: home to the Hub City Farmers Market at Harvest Park
  • Beaumont: a former mill and its adjacent mill village, a local historic district
  • Glendale: southeast of the city, near the Glendale Mill ruins

If your house is in a designated historic district, exterior changes may need approval, which can affect how a buyer plans renovations. Rain is steady through the year, so gutters, grading, crawlspace moisture and old roofs are the items a buyer's inspector will find. A seller who knows about them should plan to disclose them or price around them.

Spartanburg County School District 7 runs most city public schools, and its students are zoned to Spartanburg High School. District 6 serves the westernmost part of the city and is zoned to Paul M. Dorman High School. Your zone depends on your address, so confirm it with the district.

Inside town, SPARTA runs eight bus routes, the Amtrak Crescent stops at the Magnolia Street station and the 55-mile Daniel Morgan Trail System links trails, sidewalks and protected bike lanes.

sections.h2: Property tax due dates and appeals
sections.html:
Spartanburg County says real estate taxes are due January 15 to avoid penalties. State law adds 3 percent after the due date, another 7 percent in early February and another 5 percent in mid-March.

Tax questionSpartanburg County answer
When to pay without penaltyBy January 15
Can the tax bill itself be appealed?No, and it cannot be paid under protest
Can the appraisal be appealed?Yes, in writing to the Assessor's Office
Owner-occupied home rateMay qualify for the 4 percent assessment rate

The appraisal exists for tax purposes only, and it places no limit on what you can ask for the house.

sections.h2: What happens to taxes when a house sells
sections.html:
• The county reappraises a sold house at current market value. The 15 percent cap on increases covers only the regular reappraisals.
  • Sold this year but the bill still came to you? Pass it to the buyer or hand it to your closing attorney.
  • A sale after January 1 puts the new owner on file starting with the next tax year.

Clear any unpaid balance by closing day so the buyer gets a clean title.

sections.h2: Fees on a City of Spartanburg tax bill
sections.html:
City properties can see extra charges on the county bill. The county adds an annual landfill service charge to residential property, and the City of Spartanburg's stormwater and residential garbage fees are loaded together into a single line called the City of Spartanburg Fee Total. Questions about that line go to the city at 864-562-4510, not the county.

Ask the closing attorney to check for unpaid fees tied to the parcel. Unpaid landfill service charges become a lien on the property, ranking behind only the lien for property taxes.

South Carolina's disclosure statute asks most sellers to give a written condition statement before the buyer signs. For every topic you can write down what you know or decline to make any representation. Buyer and seller may still agree to an as-is sale, and transfers by an estate fiduciary or under a court order are exempt.

sections.h2: Preparing the house and the paperwork
sections.html:
A few small steps make any sale smoother. Start outside: clean the gutters, look under the house for moisture and study the roof from the ground. Make notes, since an inspector working for a buyer will find the same things.

On paper, gather the tax notice, a mortgage payoff figure and any letter about city fees. If a lien or an unpaid charge is attached to the parcel, learn the amount now so it can be paid from the proceeds at closing.

• Assessor's Office: appraisal questions and written appraisal appeals
  • County tax office: the bill, the January 15 deadline and payoff amounts
  • City of Spartanburg at 864-562-4510: questions about the combined Fee Total line
  • Closing attorney: how the year of sale is split and which liens must be paid

Knowing which office answers which question saves time. One notice carries both the county tax and the city's fees, yet different offices stand behind each.

Owners here turn to cash when a house needs more repair than they can pay for, when heirs live out of town, when an older mill-era house has problems an inspection will find or when a tax or fee balance keeps growing. The question is always the same: what does the house cost to keep, and what would listing cost in time and repairs?

A house in a historic district adds one more question, because exterior changes may need approval. A buyer who plans to renovate will factor that in, and a cash buyer prices it from the start.

Cash from the buyer takes the place of a mortgage lender, which means no appraisal and no loan approval holding up the date. Title, liens and the deed still go through a closing attorney. Set any written offer beside the cost and time of listing, and read the settlement statement one line at a time.

Before the first call, collect the latest tax notice, a mortgage payoff figure and anything the city mailed you about fees. An inherited house also needs the estate papers.

The usual order is simple. You describe the house, we review it as it stands and send a written offer if it fits. If you agree, you choose a closing date. The attorney clears the title, pays what you owe out of the proceeds and files the deed. You can leave behind the repairs, the repainting and the cleaning that a listing would demand.

A cash buyer will still expect an honest account of the house. Tell us about the roof, the crawlspace and any water problems, since those are the items that matter most to the price.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due on a Spartanburg house?
faqs.a: January 15 is the county's deadline to avoid penalties. After it, state law adds penalties of 3, 7 and 5 percent in stages.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Spartanburg County property tax bill?
faqs.a: Not the bill itself. Taxes cannot be appealed or paid under protest. The appraisal behind it can be challenged in writing at the Assessor's Office, and time limits apply.

faqs.q: Will the county appraisal limit what I can ask for my Spartanburg house?
faqs.a: No. The county states that its mass appraisal is done for property tax purposes only and does not restrict your asking price.

faqs.q: Why does my Spartanburg tax bill include city fees?
faqs.a: The county puts municipal fees on the notice. City stormwater and garbage charges are combined into one line, and questions about it go to the city at 864-562-4510.

faqs.q: Do I have to disclose defects when selling a house in Spartanburg?
faqs.a: Most sellers must give a written property condition statement under South Carolina law, unless the transfer is exempt. You can report what you know or say you make no representation, and a knowingly false answer can create liability.
